writtenTo: All who suffer and question God's purposes
importantNotes: Job is likely the oldest book of the Bible, set in the patriarchal period.
The book proves that suffering is not always a result of personal sin.
'I know that my Redeemer lives' (19:25) is one of the most powerful faith declarations.
God never explains to Job why he suffered — He reveals who He is instead.
Job's friends represent the 'health-and-wealth' theology that equates suffering with sin.

chapters.1: Job is introduced as righteous and blessed; Satan challenges Job's faith; Job loses everything.
chapters.2: Satan afflicts Job with painful sores; three friends come to mourn with him.
chapters.3: Job curses the day he was born and wishes he had never existed.
chapters.4: Eliphaz's first speech — he argues that suffering results from sin.
chapters.5: Eliphaz urges Job to repent and promises restoration if he turns to God.
chapters.6: Job's reply — his suffering is unbearable and his friends offer no real comfort.
chapters.7: Job laments the brevity and misery of life; he cries out to God.
chapters.8: Bildad's first speech — God is just; Job's children must have sinned.
chapters.9: Job acknowledges God's power but wonders how a mortal can argue with God.
chapters.10: Job pleads with God for answers and asks why He contends against him.
chapters.11: Zophar's first speech — God's wisdom is beyond comprehension; Job should repent.
chapters.12: Job responds that he is not inferior to his friends; God controls all things.
chapters.13: Job wants to argue his case directly before God; he rebukes his friends.
chapters.14: Job reflects on human mortality — life is short and full of trouble.
chapters.15: Eliphaz's second speech — he accuses Job of arrogance and lack of reverence.
chapters.16: Job calls his friends 'miserable comforters'; he appeals to his witness in heaven.
chapters.17: Job despairs; his spirit is broken; he sees no hope except in the grave.
chapters.18: Bildad's second speech — he describes the fate of the wicked.
chapters.19: Job's great declaration of faith: 'I know that my Redeemer lives.'
chapters.20: Zophar's second speech — the triumph of the wicked is short-lived.
chapters.21: Job argues that the wicked often prosper, contradicting his friends' theology.
chapters.22: Eliphaz's third speech — he directly accuses Job of specific sins.
chapters.23: Job yearns to find God and present his case; he trusts God's ultimate justice.
chapters.24: Job questions why God allows injustice and oppression in the world.
chapters.25: Bildad's brief third speech — no human can be righteous before God.
chapters.26: Job responds with a powerful description of God's creative power.
chapters.27: Job maintains his integrity and describes what really happens to the wicked.
chapters.28: The poem on wisdom — wisdom cannot be found except through the fear of the Lord.
chapters.29: Job recalls his former blessed and honored life.
chapters.30: Job describes his present suffering, humiliation, and rejection.
chapters.31: Job's final defense — a comprehensive oath of innocence.
chapters.32: Young Elihu speaks up, angry with both Job and his three friends.
chapters.33: Elihu argues that God speaks through suffering to turn people from sin.
chapters.34: Elihu defends God's justice — the Almighty cannot do wrong.
chapters.35: Elihu questions whether human righteousness or sin affects God.
chapters.36: Elihu proclaims God's greatness and His use of suffering for discipline.
chapters.37: Elihu points to God's power displayed in nature — storms, lightning, and weather.
chapters.38: God answers Job from the whirlwind — 'Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation?'
chapters.39: God continues describing His sovereign care over creation and the animal kingdom.
chapters.40: God challenges Job; Job is humbled. God describes the mighty Behemoth.
chapters.41: God describes the fearsome Leviathan — no one can stand against the Creator.
chapters.42: Job repents in dust and ashes; God rebukes Job's friends; Job is restored double.
